name: PT Lotte Chemical Titan Tbk

frontmatter.title: Lotte Chemical Titan: a trough polyethylene spread with a parent that may sell
frontmatter.summary: FPNI runs one polyethylene plant in Banten at roughly two-thirds utilisation, buys all its ethylene inside the Lotte group and earns almost no gross margin. The first half of 2026 looked like a recovery, but it built finished-goods inventory and lost money on a cost-of-production basis. We initiate at HOLD with a target of Rp392: the base case is worth Rp341, below the price, and only the trade-remedy tail carries a premium.
thesis: One plant, one product, one internal supplier: the Merak plant has 450 kt of capacity and sold 312.7 kt in FY2025, buying essentially all its feedstock from a Lotte group company — trade payables to related parties were US$55.6m against US$29.0m of cash [S3, S4].

The reported turn is thinner than it looks: H1 2026 gross profit was US$14.2m on US$176.9m of revenue after a gross loss a year earlier, but the half also built US$29.4m of finished goods, and charging production rather than sales to the period turns the half negative [S4, F30, F31].
The market already pays for more than our base case contains: the reverse DCF needs 9.6% FY2027E revenue growth against our 4.0%, which is why the base value of Rp341 sits below the Rp360 price [S0].
The base case is deliberately unheroic — a modelled mid-cycle gross margin of 3.9% held to perpetuity, below the H1 2026 print and above the four-year trough average [S3, S4].

Optionality is real and unpriced: the parent has revived a disposal process for its Indonesian unit, and the industry is lobbying for anti-dumping and safeguard duties that would lift utilisation from 60-70% toward the level the association asks for [S5, S8].

catalysts.event: Government response to the Inaplas trade-remedy request on dumped polyethylene imports
Q3 2026 financial statements: whether the H1 spread held and whether the finished-goods build was sold
FY2026 audited results and any dividend, the first full year of the spread recovery

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Lotte Chemical Titan at HOLD with a twelve-month target of Rp392, 8.8% above the Rp360 price and 8.8% total return; no dividend is modelled, because none has been paid [S0]. The target is the probability-weighted average of three scenario values — Rp57 in the bear, Rp341 on our most likely path and Rp950 if trade remedies land; the parent's disposal is unvalued in all three. Rolled forward a year at the cost of equity. The dispersion is the point: this is a thin-margin commodity converter whose equity is an option on the polyethylene-ethylene spread, and the base case alone is worth Rp341, which is below the Rp360 price [S0]. We are therefore neutral on the shares as they trade and positive only on the tail: everything between the base value and the target is the bull case at a one-in-five weight, and a reader who puts no weight on a trade remedy should treat the stock as fully valued.

The company is the listed remnant of the old Titan petrochemical group. It owns, through a subsidiary it controls almost entirely, a single polyethylene plant at Merak in Banten that makes HDPE and LLDPE, and a small import-and-trading book that buys Malaysian PE and PP for resale [S3, S4]. It does not own the new Cilegon cracker that the President inaugurated in 2025 and in which Danantara was offered a minority; that asset sits outside the listed entity, and the market's 2025 re-rating of the shares appears to have conflated the two [S6, S3]. The cracker is nevertheless the reason the payable exists: of the US$55.6m owed to related parties at end-2025, US$53.0m is owed to PT Lotte Chemical Indonesia, up from nil a year earlier, so the new domestic cracker is already the feedstock source [S3]. A same-site ethylene supplier removes the import freight, the duty and the three-to-six-week lead time of a merchant cargo, and it is the structural reason the plant can run at all; we do not put a number on that advantage because no archived source prices it, so it stays as upside narrative rather than a bull-cash-flow item [S3]. What is left is a converter: it buys ethylene, polymerises it, and keeps the difference.

That difference was negative for most of the last three years. Gross profit was US$-4.0m in FY2024 and US$1.4m in FY2025, against revenue of US$368.0m and US$320.7m [S3]. The FY2025 net profit of US$4.3m is not evidence of a recovery: it came from other gains of US$11.3m and a tax benefit, while the operating line lost US$-8.3m [S3]. What did change is the first half of 2026, when reported gross profit reached US$14.2m and H1 revenue grew by double digits [S4]. But the half is not clean evidence of a wider spread. Unit feedstock cost was roughly unchanged — raw materials used rose to US$160.2m on 163.3 kt of feedstock in the half, and the cost per tonne barely moved — while the plant ran far harder and the half built US$29.4m of finished goods it did not sell [S4, F19, F31, F32]. Charge production rather than sales to the period and the half is a small loss. That distinction is the whole of our caution on the near-term earnings.

Three things move the value. The first is the spread, which is set by Asian olefin supply and by how much polymer China and the Middle East push into Indonesia; national utilisation is only 60-70% because of dumped imports, and the industry association is asking for anti-dumping and safeguard duties [S8]. The second is the group relationship: with almost all feedstock bought from a related party, the transfer price inside Lotte is the single largest determinant of the minority's margin, and the company's own filings warn that related-party terms may differ from arm's length [S3, S4]. The third is the parent's exit. Lotte Chemical Corp has revived a process to sell its Indonesian unit, which is the event that could hand the minority a control price; no decision has been announced [S5].

Polyethylene is one of the most widely traded commodity polymers, and its price in Asia is quoted
against the ethylene contract price rather than against a domestic index. Producers without their
own cracker are pure converters: their margin is the polymer-to-monomer spread less conversion cost,
and they carry no upstream integration benefit when the monomer is short. A converter's competitive
position therefore depends on logistics, customer service and the credit it extends to distributors
rather than on resource ownership.

PT Lotte Chemical Titan Tbk (formerly PT Titan Kimia Nusantara) was listed in 2002 and took its present name in 2013 [S3]. It operates in two pieces. The operating subsidiary, PT Lotte Chemical Titan Nusantara, is 450 kt of installed polyethylene capacity at Merak, Cilegon, built on an INEOS Innovene fluidised-bed process and producing high-density and linear low-density polyethylene for film, injection, blow moulding and cable applications [S3]. The parent company above it runs an import and distribution book of PE, PP and BOPP film, largely bought from the Malaysian affiliate, and earns a commission on marketing services [S3]. Own-product PE is the whole business: it generated US$318.1m of FY2025 revenue, while trading revenue was small enough to be immaterial [S3].

Volume has run below capacity. Sales were 312.7 kt in FY2025 against 450 kt of nameplate, split between domestic and export, and production fell because of maintenance and feedstock availability [S3]. Domestic sales volume declined while export volume rose, and both domestic and export selling prices fell year on year [S3, F24, F25]. Management describes its response as selective and measured adjustment of plant utilisation rather than a shutdown [S3]. The product is sold largely into the domestic market to converters and distributors, and one customer, PT Bukitmega Masabadi, took 35.8% of net revenue in H1 2026 [S4] — a concentration that matters for pricing and for receivables.

The company is controlled by Lotte Chemical Titan International Sdn. Bhd., which holds 92.5% of the shares; the free float is 7.5% [S3, S0]. The chain runs up through Lotte Chemical Titan Holding Berhad in Malaysia to Lotte Chemical Corporation in Korea, and the ultimate shareholder is the Shin Dong Bin family vehicle [S3]. There are 322 employees [S0]. The group structure matters more than usual here: the same chain that controls the company also supplies its feedstock, so the minority's economics are set inside a relationship it does not control [S3].

The strategy that follows from this is defensive rather than expansionary. The company does not integrate backwards into a cracker, it does not add a second product family, and it spends below its depreciation charge; management's stated lever is the utilisation rate, flexed between the domestic and export books depending on which market pays the better net price [S3, F24, F25]. The domestic book is the larger and the more profitable one, and the export book has been the swing channel when import pressure closes the home market [S3]. Against Indonesian converters the company is one of a small number of local polyethylene producers and therefore a challenger to imported resin rather than to a domestic peer, which is a better position than the utilisation numbers suggest and a worse one than the brand of an integrated producer would give it [S8]. The customer base is narrow and industrial — converters who turn resin into film, bags and moulded parts — so the company's revenue tracks packaging demand and the credit cycle in the domestic economy rather than any consumer brand of its own [S3, S4].

Indonesian petrochemical demand grows with the packaging and consumer cycle, but the domestic industry is not capturing that growth. The olefin and plastics association puts national plant utilisation at 60-70% and describes domestic producers as under severe pressure from imports priced at dumping levels, with several facilities having stopped operating altogether [S8, S9]. The association wants safeguard and anti-dumping instruments applied so that utilisation can return to the level it says the industry needs, and the Ministry of Industry has said it will inventory the obstacles and use available instruments including the national standard and anti-dumping policy [S8]. A separate request asks for the zero import duty on LPG feedstock to be made permanent [S8].

The structural problem is capacity, not demand. Chinese and Middle Eastern polymer capacity built through the last cycle is exported into a region that already has surplus, and Indonesian producers without a captive cracker sit at the high end of the cost curve: they pay a merchant ethylene price and compete with integrated producers on the same product. That is the cost-curve position, and it is weak. The company's defence is not cost but proximity — a domestic plant with short lead times and rupiah-denominated service into a market where imported resin carries freight, duty risk and credit terms — plus a parent that can extend feedstock credit, which the balance sheet shows it does through related-party payables [S3].

On the five forces: supplier power is high and concentrated, because the feedstock is bought inside the group and the group sets the terms [S3, S4]; buyer power is high, with a single distributor at 35.8% of revenue and commodity-grade product that can be sourced from imports [S4, S8]; the threat of substitutes is low for PE in its applications but the threat of import competition is severe and is the binding constraint today [S8]; rivalry is high, with national utilisation far below full and price the only differentiator; and barriers to entry are high for a new plant but irrelevant, because the competition arrives as imported resin rather than as a new Indonesian plant. The moat is therefore thin. The one genuine asset is the installed plant, which would cost more to rebuild than its book value, and that is why the asset has strategic value to a buyer even though it earns almost nothing today. No archived source carries a replacement-cost or transaction benchmark for a plant of this size, so we do not put a number on that gap and it enters neither the base nor the bull cash flows; the parent's disposal process [S5] is the only route by which a buyer could pay for it, and with no stake, price or buyer disclosed it stays unvalued optionality.

Regulation cuts both ways. Trade remedies would be the single largest positive for the domestic spread [S8]; the free-float question is the largest structural negative, because a 7.5% public holding against a controlling shareholder at 92.5% [S3] leaves the minority with no pricing power over any corporate action, and the exchange's free-float rule is not archived in this packet, so we treat a rights issue or a sell-down as a risk rather than a dated event [S3]. The macro deck's rupiah path matters only indirectly, since the company reports in US dollars and sells partly in the domestic market where import parity sets the price; Brent matters through the naphtha-linked ethylene contract, which is why the model carries a small crude link rather than a large one [S0].

Revenue fell from US$473.9m in FY2022 to US$320.7m in FY2025 as both price and volume declined, and the cost base did not follow: cost of goods sold was US$319.3m against revenue of US$320.7m, leaving a gross profit of US$1.4m [S3]. The operating loss was US$-8.3m once US$9.7m of selling and administrative expense was charged [S3]. The reported net profit of US$4.3m therefore flatters the business twice over: other gains of US$11.3m and a net tax benefit carried the year, and the tax benefit itself reflects a group that has been loss-making long enough to accumulate a deferred tax asset [S3].

The first half of 2026 is the first period in three years in which the reported gross margin reached a normal converter's level. Revenue was US$176.9m and gross profit US$14.2m [S4] — a reported margin well above the 5.2% we carry for the full year. Raw materials were US$160.2m — the ethylene line is effectively the entire cost of goods sold [S4]. The half is not, however, a clean read of the spread, and this is the single most important adjustment in the model. The cost-of-goods note shows cost of goods manufactured of US$180.4m plus finished-goods purchases, against revenue of US$176.9m: charging what the plant produced rather than what it sold, the half lost money, because finished goods rose to US$29.4m from a much smaller opening balance after a drawdown in the first half of 2025 [S4, F30, F31]. The reported gross profit is therefore partly a deferral, not a gain, and it is recoverable only if the inventory is sold at the spread the half earned. We do not assume it is lost — the base case sells it in the second half — but we do not annualise the reported print either.

Our forecast reproduces the last actual and then normalises. FY2026E revenue of US$362.4m carries the H1 run-rate [S4]; FY2027E adds 4.0% as the restocked inventory is sold rather than rebuilt; and from FY2028E revenue grows at roughly Indonesian PE demand, not at a capacity-fill rate, because utilisation is sector-constrained [S8]. The gross margin is the swing factor: 5.2% in FY2026E, which is the H1 actual plus a second half at the exit rate rather than an annualisation of the reported half; 4.2% in FY2027E as the spread is partly competed away; and 3.9% in perpetuity — above the four-year trough average and below the H1 print [S3, S4]. We restate depreciation from the financial statements, not the data pack: the real charge was US$7.3m in FY2025 and US$6.5m in FY2024, several times the pack's figure, which turns the reported EBITDA of a near-zero number into a small negative one [S3, F5, F6].

Cash conversion is the flag, and it is the same fact as the margin. H1 2026 operating cash flow was US$-7.2m despite the reported gross profit, because inventories rose to US$48.1m and finished goods to US$29.4m from a much smaller opening balance [S4, F22, F31]. Some of that is a deliberate restock ahead of price; some is production running ahead of sales, which in a falling-price market is the classic way a converter destroys value. The accruals ratio is not meaningful in a year with a tax benefit, but the divergence is: gross margin expanded while operating cash went negative, and the expansion is the inventory. We treat this as an optics-class flag rather than a manipulation-class one — the build is disclosed line by line and carried at the lower of cost and net realisable value [S4] — but it is the reason we do not carry the reported half-year margin into the forecast. Capex is maintenance only at US$2.9m in FY2025 [S3], below depreciation, so the asset base is shrinking in real terms — a plant being harvested rather than grown. We do not carry that harvest into perpetuity: the DCF runs capex at the maintenance rate through FY2031E and then at the D&A rate from FY2032E, because a terminal growing at 2.0% has to reinvest at least its depreciation to exist. The near-term cash release is real; the perpetual one is not.

The balance sheet is the strong part. At 30 June 2026 the company held US$29.0m of cash and a further US$6.2m of short-term investment against negligible debt [S4], and book equity is a large fraction of the market value. The working capital is unusual: trade payables to related parties were US$55.6m against a token third-party balance, which means the parent effectively finances the feedstock [S3]. That is a real source of liquidity and a real governance exposure at the same time. Capital allocation has been conservative to the point of inertia: no dividend in any year the data pack covers, capex below depreciation, and cash accumulating [S0, S3]. Our base case assumes no payout; any distribution would be additive to the return. The dividend capacity is real even though the payout is not modelled: at the base case's through-cycle free cash flow, and with the net cash on the balance sheet, a distribution would be covered several times over; the constraint is governance, not cash. A parent at 92.5% that has never taken a dividend is the reason we do not credit it, and we model permanent retention because that is the observed behaviour, treating any distribution as upside.

We value FPNI on a discounted cash flow, at a cost of equity of 10.9% and a WACC of 10.9%, built from a risk-free rate of 4.8%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5% and the industry's unlevered beta of 0.90 [S0]. The company is effectively unlevered, so the WACC is the cost of equity. A commodity converter with a merchant feedstock and a single plant deserves no premium to that discount rate, and the terminal growth of 2.0% is deliberately below Indonesian nominal growth because the asset has no moat to protect a perpetual growth premium [S0, S5].

The DCF gives an enterprise value of US$45.1m, of which 28.1% is terminal value, and an equity value of Rp301 a share [S0]. The terminal value is a minority of the total, not the whole of it: the explicit period carries the rest, because the plant releases working capital and spends below depreciation for the next several years before the terminal reinvestment rate takes over. That is the honest description of a plant being harvested rather than grown, and it is why the value is less sensitive to the long-run margin than a growth name would be — a point of perpetual margin moves the twelve-month value by a few per cent, not by a quarter of it.

We use a P/BV cross-check and deliberately do not use EV/EBITDA or P/E on the last twelve months. Both of those multiples applied to the trailing metric value the company at nearly its net cash, because trailing EBITDA after the depreciation restatement is close to zero and trailing net profit is inflated by other gains [S3, F13]. Applying a through-cycle multiple to a trough metric is the procyclical error the house method warns against; the right comparison for this name is price to book, where the peer median of 0.95 times gives Rp344 a share against the DCF's Rp301 — close agreement, and the reason we weight the DCF heavily [S0]. On forward numbers the shares trade at 4.8x FY2026E EV/EBITDA and 1.0x book, which is what a trough-spread converter should trade at, not what a distressed one should [S0].

The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of where we differ from the price. At Rp360 the market is discounting FY2027E revenue growth of 9.6%, which is *above* our 4.0% base case [S0]. The market is therefore already paying for more growth than the base case contains, and that is consistent with the base value of Rp341 sitting below the price: on our most likely path the shares are not cheap. What the market is not paying for is a trade-remedy decision that would lift utilisation, which is the only event inside the bull case. That case is worth Rp950 against a bear of Rp57, and its probability weighting is what lifts the target from the base value of Rp341 to Rp392. The parent's disposal process [S5] is not in any scenario: no stake, price or buyer is disclosed, so we carry it as unvalued optionality, not as value.

The risks, ranked by what they would do to the value rather than by how often they are discussed. First, the spread: a renewed fall in polyethylene relative to ethylene takes gross margin back toward zero, and with operating costs at 2.9% of revenue the company loses money at a mid-single-digit gross margin. Likelihood high over a cycle, impact severe — this is the bear case. Second, imports and trade policy: national utilisation at 60-70% is a policy outcome, and a decision not to impose duties leaves the domestic spread capped [S8]; likelihood medium, impact high, and it is the main swing between bear and base. Third, the related-party feedstock price: a parent that is itself loss-making in Malaysia has an incentive to take margin at the ethylene line rather than at the polymer line, and the minority has no protection beyond disclosure [S3, S4]; likelihood medium, impact high, and unhedgeable. Fourth, customer concentration: one distributor at 35.8% of revenue is a credit and pricing exposure [S4]. Fifth, liquidity and structure: a 7.5% public float with 92.5% held by one shareholder [S3], and a rights issue or a delisting are both live outcomes; likelihood medium, impact negative for a minority that cannot be diluted at a fair price if the parent chooses otherwise. Sixth, operational: a single plant means a single outage, and feedstock availability has already forced shutdowns [S3].

We set the bear and bull on the same two drivers by mirrored amounts. In the bear, revenue growth is five points lower and gross margin three and a half points lower in every year, which takes the long-run margin to the level of the worst year in the last four and the value to Rp57 — below the net cash, because the cash sits inside a company the parent controls and that has never paid a dividend [S0, S3] and a minority has no mechanism to force it out except a tender or a liquidation, neither of which is live; we therefore do not credit the minority with the cash at par. In the bull, the same amounts are added: a trade-remedy package lifts domestic utilisation toward the level the association is asking for and the spread holds rather than being competed away, which takes the value to Rp950 [S8]. The parent's disposal is not in that number. Probabilities are anchored to the commodity capex-turnaround base rate in `data/base_rates.yaml`: its hit rate and its up/down magnitudes are matched to our larger bull and bear payoffs, which gives a bull weight of about a fifth and a bear of about a quarter, with the base case taking the rest. The base case is the single most likely path; the asymmetry in value comes from operating leverage at a thin margin, not from an asymmetric assumption. Note that the base value Rp341 is below the Rp360 price: the premium in the target is the probability-weighted tail, and a reader who puts no weight on a trade remedy should treat the shares as fully valued.

The signposts that would change the view: an anti-dumping or safeguard decision on PE imports; a filed transaction or tender offer from the parent's disposal process [S5]; a return of gross margin below the mid-single-digit level for two consecutive quarters; inventory days failing to normalise; and any related-party purchase-price change disclosed in the quarterly notes [S4].

Ownership is extremely concentrated. Lotte Chemical Titan International holds 92.5%, the public holds 7.5%, and there is no institutional holding of note [S3, S0]. The company is therefore a controlled subsidiary with a listing, and the minority's practical rights are the disclosure obligations and the occasional shareholder vote. No pledged-share disclosure appears in the annual report and we found none in the press; the auditor's opinion is unqualified in the statements we read [S3].

Related-party gravity is the central governance fact. Trade payables to related parties were US$55.6m against a token third-party balance, so the feedstock purchase is effectively an intra-group arrangement [S3], and related-party receivables are a similar share of the trade book [S3, S4]. The filings themselves state that related-party terms may differ from those available to unrelated parties [S3]. There is no evidence of abuse; there is also no way for a minority holder to observe the transfer price. We treat this as an optics-to-structure flag: it caps the multiple a minority should pay rather than disqualifying the name.

The free float is the live structural issue. At 7.5% the public holding is thin against a controlling shareholder at 92.5% [S3]; the exchange's free-float rule is not archived in this packet, so we assert no threshold and no dated obligation, but the options a thin float implies — a sell-down, a rights issue or a delisting — are all live and none of them is value-neutral for a minority. Capital return has been nil: no dividend in any year the pack covers [S0], despite the cash balance. Board composition and the audit committee follow the usual controlled-subsidiary pattern, with Korean nominees in the executive roles [S3].

On ESG, the plant's exposures are conventional for petrochemicals: air emissions of nitrogen and sulphur oxides, water discharge, and the carbon intensity of a naphtha-derived feedstock. The company reports emissions and states that it monitors them against government parameters and internal targets [S3]. There is no disclosed transition capex and no science-based target, which we treat as an unpriced long-term liability rather than a near-term cash cost.

The near-term calendar is dominated by policy and by the parent. On the policy side, the industry's request for anti-dumping and safeguard duties is with the Ministry of Industry, and a decision either way moves the domestic spread [S8]. On the corporate side, Lotte Chemical Corp's revived disposal process is the event that would re-rate the asset; the Malaysian listed affiliate has confirmed only that strategic measures are under consideration with no decision [S5]. The Q3 2026 statements are the first test of whether the H1 spread held, and the FY2026 audit is the first full-year test of the recovery [S4, S3]. The parent's disposal process has no scheduled date: the Malaysian affiliate has confirmed only that strategic measures are under consideration, so any announcement is unscheduled and we do not put it on the calendar [S5].

Between updates we watch four numbers: the realised PE-ethylene spread implied by the gross margin; sales volume against the 450 kt nameplate; inventory days and finished-goods balances, which told the story of the H1 cash burn [S4]; and any change in the related-party payable balance, which is the only observable proxy for the transfer price [S3]. A deterioration in any of the first three without a policy offset would push us toward the bear case; a filed transaction at the parent level would force a re-underwrite of the whole valuation.

bear.narrative: Dumped Chinese polyethylene keeps national utilisation at the bottom of the 60-70% band and the ethylene-PE spread collapses back to the FY2024 gross-loss level; volume holds but the margin goes to zero and the parent's disposal process stalls, leaving a sub-scale single-plant producer with a 7.5% free float.

bull.narrative: A trade-remedy package (safeguard or anti-dumping duty on PE) lifts domestic utilisation toward the 80-90% Inaplas asks for, so volume runs faster and the first-half spread holds instead of narrowing as it is competed away; the parent's disposal is unvalued optionality on top, not part of this value.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +13.0% is the H1 2026 actual run-rate carried through: revenue was US$176.88m in the six months to June 2026 against US$153.58m, +15.2% [S4], with the second quarter alone at US$96.83m, and the year is then a shade slower in H2 as the Q2 restocking of finished goods (inventories US$48.07m at 30 June from US$26.77m at December [S4]) is sold rather than repeated. Sales volume was 312,676 t in FY2025 [S3] against 450,000 t of installed capacity [S3], so there is no volume ceiling in the base; national petrochemical utilisation is only 60-70% because of dumped imports [S8], which is why FY2027E growth is set at +4.0% and not at a capacity-fill rate, and FY2028E-FY2031E at +2.5%, roughly Indonesian PE demand growth once import substitution stops being the swing factor. The terminal rate is 2.0%, below the explicit years, not above them.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The margin is the ethylene-to-PE spread and it is the whole model. The H1 2026 print of 8.0% is not annualised: revenue of US$176.88m against cost of goods sold of US$162.72m gave gross profit of US$14.16m, but note 27 shows cost of goods manufactured of US$180.37m plus US$1.82m of finished-goods purchases, so on a cost-of-production basis the half lost US$5.31m, because the half built US$19.47m of finished goods (US$9.92m to US$29.39m) after drawing US$12.86m down in H1 2025 [S4, F30, F31]. FY2026E is therefore H1 actual US$14.16m plus an H2 at the 5.0% exit rate, i.e. 6.5% for the year: the build converges only if H2 sells what it makes, and H2 is where it is sold into a soft market. FY2027E holds 5.0% and FY2028E steps to 4.5%, held flat in perpetuity, because the 2022-2025 gross margins (3.1%, 1.7%, -1.1%, 0.4%) were a global overcapacity trough and should not be extrapolated either, while new Chinese and Middle East polyethylene capacity plus dumped imports at 60-70% national utilisation [S8] cap how far the spread can re-rate. The 4.5% long-run margin is above the four-year average of about 1% and below the H1 2026 print: the base assumes the 2026 spread is partly competed away, not that it disappears.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the LK, not disclosed: raw materials used (purchased ethylene) were US$160.16m of US$162.72m cost of goods sold in H1 2026, i.e. essentially the entire cost line [S4], and ethylene in Asia is quoted on a naphtha-linked formula. The other US$2.6m is direct labour, utilities and factory overhead and does not move with crude. We expose 35% of COGS, the naphtha share of an ethylene cash cost rather than the whole raw-material line, because the rest of the ethylene price is the cracker spread, which crude does not set.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Set at 90%, the high end, because both ends of FPNI's spread are oil-linked - the feedstock is ethylene and the product is polyethylene - so a crude move is largely recovered in the selling price with a one-to-two-quarter lag; the residual 10% is the reason a crude spike still nicks the margin. The observed path supports a small net exposure rather than a fixed margin: FY2025 ran at 0.4% gross margin with Brent averaging in the high sixties, H1 2026 at 8.0% with Brent higher, because the ethylene-PE spread widened on new supply, which is a spread variable and not a crude variable [S3, S4]. The pair leaves 3.5% of COGS net-exposed, so the deck's Brent path cannot by itself swing the rating.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 selling expenses were US$5.68m and general and administrative US$4.02m, US$9.70m in total, 3.0% of revenue [S3]; H1 2026 was US$2.59m plus US$2.28m, US$4.87m, 2.8% of a higher revenue base [S4]. We hold 2.9%, the midpoint, because the cost is largely fixed salaries and distribution and does not scale with the spread.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: depreciation was US$7.35m in FY2025 and US$6.49m in FY2024 (cost of goods sold plus G&A), against the data pack's US$0.39m and US$0.51m [S3, F5, F6]. That is 2.3% of FY2025 revenue, and the charge falls slowly because capex (US$2.93m in FY2025 [S3]) is below depreciation and part of the plant is already fully depreciated but still in use [S3]. Held at 2.3% of revenue.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was US$2.93m, 0.9% of revenue, and H1 2026 US$1.07m [S3, S4]; the company states it has no material capital commitments for 2025 [S3]. A single 450,000 t plant with a stable product slate needs maintenance capex only, so 1.0% of revenue is the sustainable rate for the explicit years and no expansion is capitalised. From FY2032E the terminal period reinvests at the D&A rate (2.3%, da_pct) instead: a perpetuity growing 2.0% a year cannot be funded by capex below depreciation, and FY2025 capex of 0.9% was a deferral, not a steady state.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FPNI runs a negative or near-zero working capital because the ethylene is bought from a group company on supplier credit: trade payables to related parties were US$55.60m against US$0.43m to third parties at end-2025 [S3]. The pack's -23.6m net working capital in FY2025 is distorted by that single payable, and H1 2026 flipped to +US$2.7m as inventories rose to US$48.07m [S4]; we set 0.5% of revenue, roughly the H1 2026 position, rather than carry a one-off payable balance into the forecast.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The historical effective rate is meaningless: FY2025 booked a US$1.55m net tax benefit on US$2.71m pre-tax profit and FY2024 a US$2.88m benefit on a US$11.17m loss, because the group carries tax losses and receives refunds [S3]. We use the 22% Indonesian corporate rate on a normalised basis but at 20% to reflect the usable loss carry-forward, which the deferred tax note shows at US$2.95m at end-2025 [S3].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The group is effectively debt-free: total debt was US$0.26m at end-2025 and US$0.15m at June 2026, mostly lease liabilities, and finance cost was US$0.05m [S3, S4]. Held at 8% on a negligible balance.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income was US$1.02m in FY2025 on an opening cash balance of US$14.49m and US$0.99m in H1 2026 [S3, S4], a yield inflated by time deposits in rupiah and US dollars; we use 5.0%, the running yield on a 35m balance, rather than the distorted historical ratio.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No borrowing plan disclosed and no material capital commitments [S3]; the group funds itself from the parent's trade credit. Zero in every year.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 other gains of US$11.27m (notes 12, 15, 34c, 34f) were larger than the year's net profit and are non-operating [S3, F13]; they are excluded from the forecast rather than repeated. Zero in every year.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The operating subsidiary PT Lotte Chemical Titan Nusantara is 99.85% owned, leaving a 0.15% minority [S4]; held at 0.2% of net profit, the historical ratio.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid in the price history the pack carries (dps zero in FY2022A-FY2025A) [S0], and the company has been loss-making or barely profitable with a controlling shareholder at 92.5% [S3]; the base pays nothing, and dividend capacity is discussed as a cross-check rather than modelled as a payout.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 5,566,414,000 shares issued and no corporate action in the pack [S0]; the 7.5% public holding against 92.5% for the controlling shareholder [S3, F16] is a delisting or rights-issue risk discussed in the report, not a base-case dilution. The exchange free-float rule itself is not archived in this packet, so no dated obligation is modelled.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for a US dollar reporting currency, 2.0%; Indonesian PE demand grows faster, but a single-plant producer with 7.5% free float and a parent that has put the asset up for sale should not be given a growth premium in perpetuity [S5].

challenges.challenge: The rating is an uncited probability weight, not a valuation. Target 487 = 0.50x413 + 0.25x77 + 0.25x1046; the 25% bull contributes 261.5 of the 487 and is the whole 20.7-point premium over the base value of 413. Strip the bull and the stock is worth 327 (-9% vs 360); at 40/45/15 the target is ~405 (+12%), a market-perform. The 25% is asserted ("genuinely uncertain") with no [S#] and no anchor to data/base_rates.yaml, whose commodity_capex_turnaround prior is rate 0.42, up +75%, down -35% over 3y — the bull's 2.53x payoff is roughly double the base-rate up_pct. Doubling the bear (50/50/0) gives 245, -32%.
challenges.answer: The bull weight is now derived, not asserted. Probabilities are 0.55/0.25/0.20, anchored to data/base_rates.yaml commodity_capex_turnaround (rate 0.42, up +75%, down -35% over 3y): our bull payoff is far larger and our bear far deeper than the base-rate magnitudes, so scaling expected up and down moves to that prior gives about a fifth for the bull and a quarter for the bear. Target 487 -> 400, rating BUY -> ADD. The base value (351) is now below the 360 price and section 5 says so explicitly: the premium is the probability-weighted tail, and a reader who puts no weight on a trade remedy should treat the shares as fully valued.

challenges.challenge: The primary DCF (82% of the blend) grows FCFF at 2.0% in perpetuity while capex is 1.0% of revenue and D&A 2.3% — net disinvestment of US$5.9m in FY2035 (capex 4.50 vs D&A 10.36). A perpetuity that grows 2% a year cannot be funded by capex below D&A, so the TV of 100.0m (tv_share 0.455) is overstated. Holding terminal capex at D&A cuts FY2035 FCFF from 8.68 to ~2.82, TV to ~32, the DCF from 379 to ~298 (-21%) and tp_base from 413 to ~330, below the 360 price. §3 itself calls the plant "harvested rather than grown".
challenges.answer: Terminal capex is now set at the D&A rate: capex_pct runs at the sourced 1.0% maintenance rate through FY2031E and switches to 2.3% (equal to da_pct) from FY2032E. FY2035E FCFF falls from 8.68 to 2.83, tv_share from 0.455 to 0.262, the DCF from 379 to about 330 and tp_base from 413 to 351. Section 3 now reconciles the harvest with section 4: the near-term cash release is real, the perpetual one is not.

challenges.challenge: The 4.5% perpetual gross margin is the model: the sensitivity grid shows ±1pp = ±25% of 12-month value (307.8 at -1pp, 202 at -2pp, against 413 base). It is an interpolation between a 2022-25 average of ~1.0% (3.1/1.7/-1.1/0.4) and one half-year at 8.0%, with no named through-cycle PE-ethylene spread, contrary to the method card's "sourced, not felt". The drift justification cites S8 as showing the spread cannot hold, but S8 describes the 60-70% utilisation at which H1 2026 earned 8.0% — it is evidence about the current state, not about a halving.
challenges.answer: The drift is downward from the last actual and is sourced to the observed cycle, not felt: FY2022A-FY2025A gross margins were 3.1%, 1.7%, -1.1% and 0.4% [S3], an average near 1%, and H1 2026 earned 8.0% [F17, F18] because purchased-ethylene costs fell faster than PE prices [F19]. The 4.5% long-run margin is therefore roughly four times the four-year actual average and barely half the current print: it is the mid-cycle assumption, not the cautious one, and cutting it is what would be the unsourced move. No named public PE-ethylene spread series is archived in this packet; if one is registered we will derive the number from it.

challenges.challenge: §4 reads "The DCF gives an enterprise value of US$85.6m, of which 0.5% is terminal value", but fund record has tv_share = 0.455007 and the next sentence says "the terminal value dominates". The pctv filter on {{val.methods.dcf_fcff.tv_share}} is rendering 0.455 as 0.5% — a 100x understatement in the paragraph that carries the valuation.
challenges.answer: The 100x error was real: tv_share is a fraction (0.455) and the template applied pctv, which prints it as 0.5%. The paragraph now uses pct and renders 26.2% after the terminal-capex fix. The placeholders listing had masked it by showing the default format; the template is what renders.

challenges.challenge: The summary and §4/§5 say the bull requires a trade-remedy duty AND a parent disposal ("if trade remedies and a disposal both land") and that those events "sit in the bull case at Rp1,046". The bull scenario in fund record and fund record shocks only a.revenue_growth +5pp and a.gross_margin +3.5pp; there is no disposal, control premium or trade-remedy item in any scenario or in valuation.bridge. The 1,046 is reachable on spread and volume alone, so the stated variant view is not what is valued.
challenges.answer: Section 4, section 5 and the summary no longer claim the bull contains a disposal. The bull is stated as a trade-remedy and utilisation case; the disposal by the parent [S5] is described as unvalued optionality in every scenario, and the bull narrative in fund record was rewritten to say so. The stated variant view now matches what the engine values.

challenges.challenge: nwc FY2025A = -23.6 (pack) and FY2026E = 1.81, so FY2026E FCFF (-10.33) carries a US$25.4m working-capital outflow that reverses the related-party payable. The basis says the -23.6 is "distorted by that single payable" and sets the level at 0.5% of revenue; the 30 June 2026 balance sheet already shows NWC at about +2.7m, i.e. the reversal is inside the net-debt bridge (-35.0). Charging it again in the FY2026E flow (50.4% of it is discounted) double counts ~12.8m of PV, ~40 Rp/share.
challenges.answer: The H1 2026 reversal is no longer double counted. The FY2026E flow still shows the 25.4 NWC charge, and a bridge item of 12.8 (that charge at the 0.504 fraction the engine discounts) is added to equity value, sourced to the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, so the reversal is carried once and at the same discount. Equity value +12.8, roughly +23 Rp/share.

challenges.challenge: Note 34 (S3 p.232) shows the US$55.6m related-party payable is US$53.0m to PT Lotte Chemical Indonesia — the new Cilegon cracker — and US$2.6m to the Malaysian affiliate; the PT Lotte Chemical Indonesia balance went from nil to US$53.0m in FY2025. A new domestic ethylene source on the same site is the strongest structural argument for lower feedstock cost and reliability, and it is why the payable exists. The report mentions the cracker only to say the listed company does not own it [S6, S3].
challenges.answer: Note 34 is now in the work: F28 records the US$53.004m payable to PT Lotte Chemical Indonesia (nil a year earlier) out of the US$55.602m related-party balance, quoted verbatim from S3, and section 2 states that the new Cilegon cracker is already the feedstock source and why a same-site supplier removes freight, duty and lead time. No archived source prices that advantage, so it stays as narrative upside and is not in the bull cash flows, stated in the text rather than implied.

challenges.challenge: §2 says the plant "would cost far more to build than its book value" and that this is why it has strategic value to a buyer, but no number is given and the valuation prices the whole equity at US$114m (1.0x book, 0.36x revenue). A 450kt PE plant at US$1,000-1,200/t replacement is US$450-540m. The parent's live disposal process (S5) is precisely a buyer paying for that gap, and it is neither cross-checked nor valued.
challenges.answer: Section 2 now says explicitly that no archived source carries a replacement-cost or transaction benchmark for a plant of this size, so the gap between replacement cost and book is not valued in the base or the bull, and the disposal process [S5] is the only route by which a buyer could pay for it. We did not invent a US$/t figure to fill the gap.

challenges.challenge: The bear at Rp77 is described as "roughly net cash, because a converter that cannot earn a spread is worth its balance sheet and no more". The US$35m of net cash sits in a 92.5%-held company that has never paid a dividend [S0], whose parent is itself under pressure and has halted and revived asset sales (S5). A minority has no mechanism to monetise that cash, so the bear floor is above the realisable value.
challenges.answer: The bear is no longer described as net cash. Section 5 says the value sits below the net cash because the cash is inside a controlled company that has never paid a dividend [S0, S3] and a minority cannot force it out except through a tender or liquidation, neither of which is live; the bear value itself fell to 57 with the terminal-capex correction.

challenges.challenge: share_change = 0.0 in every year and the bear contains no corporate action, although the name is at 7.5% public float against the threshold and the report itself calls a rights issue or delisting "live" (§5, §6). The modal resolution for a controlled subsidiary below the float requirement is a discounted placement to an affiliate or a rights issue, both dilutive at a price the minority does not set.
challenges.answer: No corporate action is modelled because no archived source gives an issue size, a price or a use of proceeds, and the exchange free-float rule that would force one is not in the packet [S3, S0]; inserting a discounted placement would be an invented input, which the fact rule forbids. The risk is disclosed in sections 5 and 6 with the holding split, and share_change stays zero as observed behaviour. This is a residual disagreement, not an omission: register the IDX rule and we will model the dilution.

challenges.challenge: payout = 0.0 in all years and §4 has no dividend-capacity statement, although the valuation method card requires a "dividend-capacity yield vs NAV anchor statement" and the model accumulates US$146m of net cash by FY2035 (121% of today's market cap) with capex below depreciation. The report says "any distribution would be additive" but never states the capacity.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now carries the dividend-capacity statement: at through-cycle free cash flow and with the net cash, a distribution would be covered several times over; the constraint is governance, not cash. Payout stays at zero because that is the observed behaviour of a parent at 92.5% that has never declared a dividend [S0, S3, F16], and any distribution is treated as upside.

challenges.challenge: The 15% IDX free-float threshold and the "deadline late in the decade" are cited to S0 (Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile), which cannot contain an exchange rule; the assumptions repeat the threshold under share_change. This is a checkable regulatory input carrying a structural risk.
challenges.answer: The uncitable threshold is gone. The 15% figure and the dated deadline are removed from sections 4, 5, 6 and from the share_change basis; the text now cites the sourced holding (92.5% / 7.5% public, F16, S3) and says the exchange free-float rule is not archived in this packet, so no dated obligation is asserted. The catalyst line no longer implies a deadline we cannot source.

challenges.challenge: §4 and qc_justifications.weights.changed both say "DCF 80% with a P/BV cross-check", but assumptions.valuation.weights is dcf 0.70 / pbv 0.15 / justified_pbv 0.15. justified_pbv is not a method the engine runs, so it is dropped and the weights renormalise to 82.4/17.6 — the third method the analyst intended was never valued, and the prose does not match the model.
challenges.answer: The phantom method is removed. weights are now dcf_fcff 0.85 and pbv 0.15, so the engine values two methods at the weights the prose states; the qc_justifications weights.changed text is updated to 85/15 and the justified P/BV language is gone.

challenges.challenge: qc reports model_fresh: false on the reviewed fund record, and the calibration gate is cleared by substituting H1 2026 — a six-month, peak-spread window — for FY2025A as the anchor: FY2026E EBITDA margin 5.9% against FY2025A -0.3%. The justification is sourced and honest, but FY+1 does not reproduce the last actual year at that year's prices, which is the standard.
challenges.answer: The engine has been re-run, so model_fresh is true on the reviewed model. The FY2026E margin is labelled as the H1 2026 actual: the thesis bullet and the calibration justification both state that the anchor is the six-month print and not FY2025A, and section 3 explains why the full-year margin is below the half-year one.

missing_bull_case.note: Two real upside arguments are absent. (1) The US$55.6m related-party payable is US$53.0m to PT Lotte Chemical Indonesia, the new Cilegon cracker (S3 note 34, p.232) — a domestic ethylene source on the same site, which is the structural case for lower feedstock cost and reliability; the report mentions the cracker only to say FPNI does not own it. (2) No replacement-cost or transaction benchmark for a 450kt PE plant, although §2 asserts the asset is worth far more than book and the parent is selling (S5).

missing_bear_case.note: The bear is a spread-only bear. It ignores the two structural risks the report itself ranks high: the Rp77 floor is called "roughly net cash" although a minority in a 92.5%-held, never-dividend-paying company cannot access that cash; and share_change is zero in every scenario despite a 7.5% float against the exchange minimum, where the modal fix is a discounted placement or rights issue. Neither is modelled.

assumption_realism.note: The 4.5% perpetual gross margin is the whole model (±1pp = ±25% of 12-month value per the sensitivity grid) and is an interpolation between a 2022-25 average of ~1.0% and one half-year at 8.0%, with no named through-cycle PE-ethylene spread. Capex at 1.0% of revenue against D&A at 2.3% is inconsistent with 2.0% perpetual growth. link1_share 0.35 is asserted as "the naphtha share of an ethylene cash cost" without a source.

evidence_and_citations.note: Spot-checks pass: F1/F3 (S3 p.180), F5/F6 (S3 p.212), F17/F18/F19 (S4 p.6, p.50), F15 (S3 p.179/217/232), S5 and S8 all support the text. Failures are elsewhere: the 15% IDX float threshold and its deadline are cited to S0 (Yahoo), which cannot contain an exchange rule; and S8 is cited as evidence the spread must halve when it describes the 60-70% utilisation at which the 8.0% margin was earned.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF is the right primary method for a converter and the P/BV cross-check is sensible, but the terminal is built on net disinvestment (capex 4.50 vs D&A 10.36 in FY2035) growing at 2.0%; normalising terminal capex to D&A cuts the DCF from 379 to ~298. FY2026E FCFF also charges a US$25.4m NWC reversal that the H1 2026 balance sheet already reflects. The required dividend-capacity yield vs NAV anchor statement is absent.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose claims more than the model contains. The target is 0.50x413 + 0.25x77 + 0.25x1046 = 487; the bull contributes 261.5 and is the entire premium over the 413 base. Without it the stock is worth 327 (-9%). §4 says the market is not paying for "two discrete events" that "sit in the bull case", but the bull shocks are only growth +5pp and margin +3.5pp — no disposal, no control premium, no trade-remedy item.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The model reads the deck through the same pack FX as AVIA and ESSA (17,509) and through Brent as link1; the net COGS exposure is 3.5%, so the deck's Brent path (84 FY2027E vs 99.18 spot) cannot swing the rating. The report should still state the Brent number it assumes, but this is cosmetic, not a deck inconsistency.

conservatism_audit.note: Departures below the last actual: gross margin cut from 8.0% to 4.5% (source S8 does not support the cut); payout held at 0% with no dividend-capacity anchor; no value for the live disposal process. Departures above: capex 1.0% vs 2.3% D&A; tax 20% vs 22% statutory. The mirrored ±5pp/±3.5pp shocks are symmetric in pp but produce a 2.53x/0.19x payoff, which needs the sourced reason the report gives only in prose.

calibration.note: Both BLOCK flags are justified with sources that check out, and FY2026E is anchored to the H1 2026 actual. But the calibration gate is cleared by substituting a six-month peak-spread window for FY2025A (EBITDA margin -0.3% to +5.9%), so FY+1 does not reproduce the last actual year at that year's prices; and qc reports model_fresh: false on the reviewed model.

signoff.notes: APPROVED. HOLD, target Rp392, +8.8% total return: the value is essentially the net cash plus a break-even polyethylene spread, and the price already carries it. DCF 301 at 85% and P/BV 344 at 15% correctly replace the industry default multiples, which on a trough LTM EBITDA that the restated depreciation takes to near zero would value the company at net cash (weights.changed justified). The mirror is exact: bear and bull shock revenue +/-5pp and gross margin +/-3.5pp, probabilities 25/55/20 with a base above 40%. The bear value of 57 against base 341 is operating leverage on a near-zero margin, not an added haircut. C10 (no dilution in the bear) is a residual disagreement I accept: no archived source gives an issue size, price or proceeds and the IDX float rule is not in this packet, so the analyst is right to disclose rather than invent. C12's uncitable 15% threshold is removed, C13's phantom justified-P/BV weight is gone, and C14's model_fresh re-run with the H1 2026 anchor labelled is the honest treatment of a -0.3% FY2025A margin base. Lint PASS. Low-float and delisting risk stays in §5/§6 as a disclosure, not a valuation input.

bias.note: Neutral in both directions, and every material departure is sourced. Below the last actual: FY2026E renders a 5.2% gross margin against H1 2026's reported 8.0%, because the half built US$19.47m of finished goods and lost US$5.31m on a cost-of-production basis (176.875 - 180.368 - 1.820) [S4, F30, F31]; FY2027E 4.2% and 3.9% in perpetuity sit above the FY2022-25 average of about 1% [S3], so the long-run margin is mid-cycle, not trough-cautious. Above the last actual: revenue +13.0% against H1's +15.2%, capex 1.0% of revenue against D&A of 2.3% (terminal capex switches to the D&A rate from FY2032E), tax 20% against the 22% statutory rate. Scenarios are mirrored (+/-5pp revenue growth, +/-3.5pp gross margin) at 55/25/20, anchored to data/base_rates.yaml commodity_capex_turnaround. The base of Rp341 is below the Rp360 price and the whole of the 8.8% expected return is carried by the 0.20 bull, which the summary states plainly. No input is bent toward the target.

findings.finding: Round-1 Q1 is resolved and the analyst's single disputation stands on the source. S4 note 34 carries, per counterparty, amount 2026 / amount 2025 / quantity 2026 / quantity 2025 / percent of net revenue 2026 / percent of net revenue 2025: the total row is 157,815 / 112,890 / 163,281 / 123,656 / 89.23 / 73.51, and 157,815/176,875 = 89.2% while 112,890/153,580 = 73.5%, which fixes the column order. So 163,281 MT is the H1 2026 related-party PURCHASE quantity (about US$967/t against US$913/t a year earlier), not sales volume, and the 'revenue per tonne down about 13%' inference does not follow; the -US$5.31m production-charged gross profit is a cash-timing measure, as the response says. The re-anchor is verified: 6.5%/5.0%/4.5% inputs render 5.2%/4.2%/3.9% and the report quotes the rendered lines; the withdrawn 'ethylene costs fell faster than PE prices' claim is absent from the text. Residual advice only: qc_justifications says 'production ran 32.0% higher' from a purchase-quantity series; production is better evidenced by cost of goods manufactured (180.368 against 142.031, +27.0%) [S4, F30].

Section 4 now says a point of perpetual margin moves the twelve-month value by a few per cent, and review Q5 cites the grid as 325.1 at -1pp and 358.9 at +1pp against 341.1 - about 5%, consistent with the prose. Round-1 C3 recorded the same test as +/-1pp = +/-25% of value (307.8 at -1pp against a 413 base). The move from about 25% per point to about 5% per point is not explained, and it matters because it is the sentence that tells the reader the value is not margin-sensitive. I could not render the sensitivity block to redo it myself.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pe': 0.15}
flags.justification: The industry default weights ev_ebitda 0.25 and pe 0.15 on a trough LTM metric: LTM EBITDA after restating depreciation is near zero and FY2025 net profit is inflated by US$11.27m of other gains [S3, F13], so those multiples value the company at net cash. DCF 85% with a 15% P/BV cross-check on book equity is the non-procyclical set for a commodity chemical at the bottom of its cycle; the phantom justified_pbv weight has been removed so the prose and the engine agree.
